content: Omeprazole can cause a condition called hypomagnesemia, which refers to low magnesium levels in the blood. This can lead to serious complications, including seizures and irregular heart rhythms. Individuals who take omeprazole for extended periods or concurrently with other medications that lower magnesium levels are at a higher risk. If you experience symptoms such as changes in heart rate or rhythm (e.g., rapid or skipped heartbeats), dizziness, muscle spasms, or seizures, you should stop taking omeprazole and contact your healthcare provider immediately. Omeprazole use has been associated with bone loss and an increased risk of fractures, particularly in older adults and those taking high doses or using the medication long-term. This risk should be carefully considered, especially in populations at higher risk for osteoporosis or fractures. Severe allergic reactions to omeprazole can occur and may be life-threatening. Symptoms of a serious allergic reaction include difficulty breathing or wheezing, a racing heart, fever, swollen lymph nodes, swelling of the face, lips, mouth, tongue, or throat, trouble swallowing, throat tightness, itching, skin rash, hives, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, fainting, stomach cramps, or joint pain. If you experience any of these symptoms, stop taking omeprazole and seek immediate medical attention. Omeprazole can cause kidney problems, including a condition called acute tubulointerstitial nephritis, which can occur at any time during treatment. Symptoms such as reduced urine output or blood in the urine should prompt immediate medical evaluation. The use of omeprazole has been linked to an overgrowth of the bacterium Clostridioides difficile in the gut, which can result in severe diarrhea. Symptoms include watery diarrhea, persistent diarrhea, blood in the stool, severe abdominal cramps, and fever. If these symptoms occur, contact your healthcare provider promptly. Severe skin reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN), have been reported with omeprazole use. These conditions can be life-threatening if untreated. Symptoms include painful red or purple skin that appears burned and peels, flat red rashes or blisters on the skin, mouth, nose, or genitals, and red, painful, watery eyes. If you develop a rash or any of these symptoms, stop taking omeprazole and seek emergency medical care. Omeprazole can also cause a rare but serious allergic reaction called DRESS (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms), which can affect multiple organs, including the liver, kidneys, and heart. Symptoms of DRESS include skin rash, hives, fever, swollen lymph nodes, shortness of breath, swelling in the legs or feet, dark urine, or yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice). If you experience any of these symptoms, discontinue the medication and seek immediate medical attention. In some cases, omeprazole may trigger or worsen lupus, an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks the body’s own tissues. Symptoms such as new or worsening joint pain or a rash on the arms or cheeks should be reported to your healthcare provider immediately. Long-term use of omeprazole (three years or more) can lead to vitamin B12 deficiency, as the medication reduces the absorption of this essential vitamin. Symptoms of B12 deficiency include a sore tongue, weakness, tingling, or numbness in the hands or feet. If you experience these symptoms, consult your healthcare provider. Omeprazole should only be used under the guidance of a healthcare provider. It is not intended for immediate relief of heartburn, as it may take 1 to 4 days to achieve its full effect. The medication should be taken as prescribed, and capsules should not be chewed, cut, or crushed. If swallowing capsules is difficult, the contents can be sprinkled on a tablespoon of applesauce and swallowed immediately without mixing with other foods. Before starting omeprazole, inform your healthcare provider about all your medical conditions, including low potassium (hypokalemia), low magnesium (hypomagnesemia), low calcium (hypocalcemia), or liver problems. Additionally, disclose all medications, supplements, and herbal products you are taking, as omeprazole can interact with other drugs, potentially altering their effectiveness or causing adverse effects. Pregnant individuals should consult their healthcare provider before using omeprazole, as its effects on pregnancy and the unborn baby are not fully understood. Breastfeeding individuals should avoid omeprazole, as it can pass into breast milk. If you miss a dose of omeprazole, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take double doses to make up for a missed dose. In the event of an overdose, seek immediate medical attention by calling 911 or contacting a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222. Common side effects of omeprazole include headache, stomach pain, nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, gas, and, in children aged 1 to 16 years, infections of the nose or throat and fever. If these side effects persist or worsen, inform your healthcare provider. Serious side effects should be reported to the FDA at 800-FDA-1088 or Health Canada at 866-234-2345.
